The National Pension Commission has disclosed that only 14 of Nigeria’s 36 states are paying pensions regularly, acknowledging that some state governments are performing poorly in meeting their obligations to retirees. The Director-General of PenCom, Omolola Oloworaran, made this known during an interview with ARISE NEWS on Monday, describing pension payments as a continuing challenge in several states. “We have 14 states that are paying up. But 14 out of 36 states is a lot. And some states are doing very badly,” she said. However, she did not name the 14 states that are making regular pension payments or identify the states defaulting on their obligations. ₦400bn pension fund can sustain minimum payments for 10 years — PenCom Oloworaran also said the ₦400bn provided by the Federal Government and the pension industry for the Pension Protection Fund could sustain the minimum monthly pension initiative for at least 10 years, based on current projections. She said the government contributed ₦350bn, while the pension industry provided ₦50bn. Speaking during the interview, she explained that the commission had engaged an actuary to assess the cost of the initiative and project its long-term sustainability. “Conservatively, we’re good for the next 10 years. Conservatively,” she said. Make PUNCH part of your everyday experience. She said the commission was committed to ensuring that vulnerable retirees continued to receive financial support through the minimum pension arrangement. The PenCom boss also disclosed that the Pension Protection Fund had ₦38bn before the current administration, adding that the Federal Government’s contribution included payments to clear outstanding pension backlogs. She said 54 per cent of beneficiaries who had received payments under the initiative were private-sector retirees, while nearly 70 per cent of workers expected to qualify were in the private sector. Police pension dispute On the dispute involving retired police officers seeking to exit the Contributory Pension Scheme and return to a defined-benefit arrangement, Oloworaran said the commission was working with the police to develop a solution that would protect their retirement funds. She disclosed that different options had been presented to President Bola Tinubu for consideration, adding that the priority was to ensure that police retirees received improved pension benefits. “But what we want to do is put a structure in place. Where we are sure that nothing at all will happen to the funds for our police,” she said. Oloworaran said the ultimate objective was to ensure that retired police officers received more money, regardless of the pension arrangement eventually adopted. “And the ultimate result is more money in the hands of police. Whether you do it in the scheme or outside the scheme, it doesn’t matter,” she said. She expressed hope that the dispute would be resolved before the end of the year, although she acknowledged that government bureaucracy could delay the process. “I’m hoping, I mean, government is tough. A lot of bureaucracy here and there. I’m hoping before the end of the year, we would have resolved the police issue,” she said. Tinubu had launched the ₦52,500 monthly minimum pension guarantee on November 10, 2026, for 173,209 eligible retirees under the Contributory Pension Scheme, ending a 22-year delay in implementing the provision of the Pension Reform Act. He also inaugurated the Pension Industry Healthcare Plan for Retirees (PenCare), which is designed to provide free essential healthcare services to low-income pensioners. The initiatives were unveiled at a ceremony in Abuja, where he was represented by Senate President Godswill Akpabio.
